summary: Specifies a certificate extension that lets public key certificates and attribute certificates include logotypes. It obsoletes RFCs 3709 and 6170.

eli5.summary: A digital ID card can carry a little logo picture of the organization that it belongs to.

questions: how to add a logo to a certificate
what is the x.509 logotype extension
what image formats can certificate logotypes use
subtitle: How a certificate can carry a logo of its issuer, its owner or a community, purely to help people recognize it.

tldr.problem: Certificates are built for machines, and the screens that show them to people are technical and hard to find. People recognize logos and brands far more readily than certificate fields.
tldr.mechanism: A non-critical X.509 certificate extension carries logotypes (images and optional audio) either by reference, as a URI plus a one-way hash, or embedded directly with a data URI. Clients check the hash and show the logo only for certificates that validate.
tldr.outcome: Logotypes are display aids only and MUST NOT take part in path validation or automated trust decisions. This document merges and obsoletes RFC 3709 and RFC 6170.

facts.label: Recommended image size
facts.value: at least one image 60 to 200 px wide and 45 to 150 px high

today: RFC 9399 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2023. It obsoletes RFC 3709 and RFC 6170, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Put Logos in Certificates
sections.content:
A certificate binds a public key to the identity of its subject. Most of what it holds suits machine processing, not the human process of recognizing and trusting something. The RFC notes that people tend to trust what they recognize, and that physical identification cards already use logotypes and symbols to help with exactly that.

It names two situations. First, a user may look at the result of a certificate-based identification, but viewing a certificate is often hard to find and too technical to read. Second, a user may have to pick one certificate from several, much like choosing a plastic card from a wallet, where color and branding help.

The RFC supplements RFC 5280 (public key certificates) and RFC 5755 (attribute certificates). It obsoletes RFC 3709 and RFC 6170.

The logotype extension MUST NOT be an active component in automated certification path validation. Logos are for humans only.
sections.eli5: Grown-ups often recognize a card by its picture, like a bank logo, long before they read the small print. Putting a logo on a digital ID helps people recognize it the same way.

sections.title: Kinds of Logotypes and Their Data
sections.content:
The RFC defines three standard logotype types: a community logotype, an issuer organization logotype and a subject organization logotype. A community logotype is a general mark for a community, such as a global brand that local issuers co-brand with. The other two represent the organization named in the issuer name or the subject name of the certificate. Other types can be added, each identified by an object identifier.

Logotype data is either image or audio. Implementations MUST support image data, while audio support is OPTIONAL. Every logotype MUST be represented by at least one image object, and at least one image object SHOULD have a width between 60 and 200 pixels and a height between 45 and 150 pixels.

One logotype may have several image or audio objects in different formats, sizes or languages, and the issuer must make sure they carry roughly the same content. Applications MUST NOT display more than one image object, or play more than one audio object, for the same logotype type at the same time. Clients SHOULD cache logotype data.
sections.eli5: A badge can show the club that made it, the person who owns it, or a big group both belong to. You may have a small and a big copy of the same picture, but you only hang up one of them.

sections.title: Direct and Indirect Addressing
sections.content:
Logotype data can be pointed to in two ways. With direct addressing, the certificate describes each image or audio object and lists the URIs where it can be fetched, together with one or more one-way hashes. With indirect addressing, the certificate points to an external, hashed structure that lists the type, content and location of many alternative objects.

Certificate issuing applications MUST support direct addressing and SHOULD support indirect addressing. Client applications SHOULD support both. Several URIs may be given for the same data to improve availability, and a client that cannot fetch from one SHOULD try another. Clients MUST support retrieval over HTTP or HTTP with TLS, and SHOULD support the data URI scheme for embedded data. The data scheme MUST NOT be used with indirect addressing.

Every referenced object has a hash computed on the whole object. CAs MUST use the hash function associated with the certificate signature for one hash value and MAY add others. Clients MUST compute a hash with one of the listed functions and MUST discard the logotype data if it does not match.
sections.eli5: The card can either hold the picture itself, or hold a note saying where to find it plus a fingerprint of the picture. If the picture you find does not match the fingerprint, you throw it away.

sections.title: The Logotype Extension
sections.content:
The extension is identified by id-pe-logotype (arc id-pe value 12) and MAY appear in public key certificates or attribute certificates. It MUST NOT be marked critical, so a client that does not understand it can simply carry on. At least one of the optional elements of LogotypeExtn MUST be present.

The structure has four optional parts: communityLogos (a sequence, most preferred first), issuerLogo, subjectLogo and otherLogos. Each is a LogotypeInfo, which is either direct data or an indirect reference. Each image or audio object has a mediaType, a list of hashes and a list of URIs. Optional image details give the type (gray scale or color), file size, recommended xSize and ySize, and a language tag. If a recommended size differs from the real image, the image SHOULD be scaled to fit while keeping its ratio.

The issuer logo MUST be consistent with, and require, an organization name in the issuer field. The subject logo has the same rule for the subject field. The relationship between a logo and its organization is asserted by the issuer, and how an issuer checks it is outside the scope of the RFC.

Three further logotypes are defined for otherLogos: a loyalty logotype (there MAY be several), a certificate background logotype that must let black text be read on top of it, and a certificate image logotype, which MUST be a complete visual representation of the certificate. There MUST NOT be more than one background or certificate image logotype.
sections.eli5: The extension is a form with slots for: the club's badge, the issuer's badge, the owner's badge, and extra badges. You fill in at least one slot, and nothing breaks if a reader does not know the form.

sections.title: Embedded Data and Media Formats
sections.content:
A logotype image may be stored inside the extension using the data URI scheme. The mediaType in the extension MUST be identical to the media type in the data URL, and the hash is calculated over the same data as for an external file. The RFC cautions that implementations must watch the size of embedded images so the certificate stays usable.

For images, JPEG, GIF and compressed SVG (image/svg+xml+gzip) MUST be supported. SVG and PNG SHOULD be supported and PDF is optional. Animated images SHOULD NOT be used. SVG must follow the SVG Tiny profile, must not contain script elements or references to outside data, and is hashed over its uncompressed content with linefeed line endings. PDF, if used, MUST follow PDF/A.

For audio, implementations that support it MUST support MP3 (audio/mpeg) and SHOULD support text-based audio (text/plain;charset=UTF-8) for text-to-speech software. For text-based audio, the language MUST be given and the file size, play time and channels fields MUST be 0.
sections.eli5: You can tuck a tiny picture right inside the card, or keep it elsewhere. Only some picture types are allowed so every reader can open them safely, and the pictures are not allowed to run programs.

sections.title: How Clients Use Logotypes
sections.content:
Logotypes are used at the discretion of the issuer and the client, and the relying party MUST NOT use them for certification path validation or automated trust decisions. A client MAY, under local policy, show none, one or several of the logotypes, and MAY combine image and audio freely, although it MUST NOT play more than one audio sequence at once.

If a client cannot support a logotype it MUST NOT report an error, and behaves as if the extension were absent. Clients MUST be able to disable fetching of logotypes, while cached ones may still be shown. The logotype is shown together with the other identity information, never instead of it.

If the relying party cannot successfully validate the certificate, it MUST NOT display any logotype data associated with it.
sections.eli5: Your app may show the badge, or not, or only some badges. If the card turns out to be fake, it must not show the badge at all.

sections.title: Security Risks of Logos
sections.content:
The RFC admits that logotypes are very difficult to define securely: it is hard to say what is a legitimate logotype of an organization, and checking can be costly. A dishonest or careless issuer could issue a certificate with names and logos it has no claim to, so a logotype is trusted only if the certificate validates in a valid path, and an invalid certificate must get no help from its logo.

A parent CA cannot technically stop a subordinate CA from including inappropriate logotypes, since path processing does not constrain them. The RFC lists non-technical controls: contracts, monitoring including Certificate Transparency, certificate policies and revocation.

Other points include hash-covered images that pull in external data (clients SHOULD reject SVG images with external references), caution about embedded images when the signature hash is vulnerable to collision attacks, and a media type that does not match the HTTP Content-Type, which MUST be treated as a failure.
sections.eli5: Anyone can draw a fake logo, so a badge only counts if the card itself checks out. The people who hand out cards have to be trusted, and a few rules help keep fake badges out.

sections.title: Privacy When Fetching Logos
sections.content:
Certificates are commonly public, so privacy-sensitive information should be avoided in them. When logotype data is fetched from a server, a network observer or the server operator can learn which clients use certificates with particular logotype data. Local caching reduces this, and the cache index should use the hash values so the same data is fetched only once even if several URIs name it.

Embedding the logo with the data URI scheme and direct addressing avoids any fetch, at the cost of a larger certificate. Privacy-aware subscribers MAY insist on it. When fetching remotely, relying parties should avoid cookies, ETags and client certificates to limit fingerprinting. The RFC also points out that with TLS 1.3 a client fetching remote logotype data could disclose an otherwise encrypted server identity.
sections.eli5: If you have to ask a stranger for the picture every time, they learn where you have been. Keeping the picture inside the card, or keeping a copy at home, tells nobody anything.
